Vulture
vŭl'chər
n. (a carrion bird of the unclean list; and in Job the possessor of the keenest eye in creation, which still cannot find wisdom)
Latin vultur. The Hebrew daah and dayyah name birds of prey; ayyah at Job 28:7 is rendered vulture, and the passage turns entirely on the sharpness of the creature's sight.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

In the law: “And the vulture, and the kite after his kind” (Lev 11:14), and in the rehearsal, “And the glede, and the kite, and the vulture after his kind” (Deu 14:13), among the fowls Israel was to have in abomination (Lev 11:13). But the great use is in Job's hymn to wisdom. Chapter 28 describes men mining — sinking shafts, cutting rivers among the rocks, bringing to light things hid — and then says of the way to wisdom: “There is a path which no fowl knoweth, and which the vulture's eye hath not seen” (Job 28:7). The vulture is the proverbial far-seer, and its eye has not found this road. The chapter presses the question — “But where shall wisdom be found? and where is the place of understanding?” (Job 28:12) — through the deep and the sea and the price of gold, and answers it at last from outside the search altogether: “Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding” (Job 28:28).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines the vulture as a rapacious fowl of the genus Vultur, which feeds chiefly on carrion, remarkable for its keenness of sight and smell.

expand to see more

VULTURE, n. [L. vultur.] A genus of rapacious fowls.

The vulture feeds chiefly on carrion, and is remarkable for the acuteness of its sight and smell.

Which the vulture's eye hath not seen. Job xxviii.

VULTURINE, a. Belonging to a vulture; rapacious.

Key Scripture

Job 28:7 — "There is a path which no fowl knoweth, and which the vulture's eye hath not seen:"

Job 28:12 — "But where shall wisdom be found? and where is the place of understanding?"

Job 28:28 — "And unto man he said, Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding."

Lev 11:14 — "And the vulture, and the kite after his kind;"

Modern Corruption

Wisdom is sought as information to be discovered, and Job 28 says the sharpest eye in creation has not found the path and that God gave the answer by speaking.

expand to see more

Job 28 is the most sustained argument in Scripture about the limits of investigation, and it is not hostile to investigation at all. The chapter opens by admiring it: men have a vein for silver and a place for gold, they put an end to darkness, they cut out rivers among the rocks, and the earth's hidden things are brought to light. What it denies is that the same method reaches wisdom. The path is one no fowl knows and the vulture's eye has not seen; the deep says it is not in me, the sea says it is not with me; it cannot be gotten for gold, nor valued with the precious onyx. That is a direct contradiction of the working assumption of a scientific age, which is that everything worth knowing is in principle findable by search. Some things are found only because they are told, and the chapter ends with God telling.

The answer, when it comes, is startling for its plainness after twenty-seven verses of unreachable places: Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding. Wisdom turns out not to be an elite attainment but a stance available to any man, and it has two parts, one Godward and one moral. The vulture's eye is superb and useless here; a farmer in the fear of God has what the bird cannot see. That is also why the New Testament locates wisdom in a Person — Christ, in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, and who is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption. The path was never going to be spotted from the air. It had to be revealed, and it was.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ayyah (H344), rendered vulture at Job 28:7; daah (H1676) and dayyah (H1772) in the law; with chokmah (H2451), wisdom.

expand to see more

Hebrew ayyah (H344) — a bird of prey of keen sight; which the vulture's eye hath not seen; Job 28:7.

Hebrew daah (H1676) — a bird of prey, rendered vulture; Leviticus 11:14.

Hebrew nathib (H5410) — a path, a beaten track; there is a path which no fowl knoweth; Job 28:7.

Hebrew chokmah (H2451) — wisdom; where shall wisdom be found; Job 28:12.

Hebrew yirah (H3374) — fear, reverence; the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom; Job 28:28.

Usage

"“Which the vulture's eye hath not seen” — the sharpest sight in creation, and it misses the road."

"“Where shall wisdom be found?” — asked after the deep and the sea have both answered no."

"“The fear of the Lord, that is wisdom” — told, because it could not be found."
